article.title: No to abolition
article.author: Socialist Forum
article.content: Editorial note: The following is a letter response to Hazel W.’s piece, “ In Defense of Abolition .” In July, the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) amended its program to call for “abolishing the police and prison system.” Taken literally, that is a mistake. Society needs institutions to patrol and isolate the dangerous few. Even the most radical socialist societies understood this. For example, the Paris Commune — that libertarian-left experiment — had a prefecture of police. It established neighborhood watches and incarcerated thousands as “hostages of the people of Paris.” The commune is not proof of concept for prison and police abolition. It is stark evidence of just how foundational, including under socialism, those institutions are. Even the society you might least expect to have a carceral system did not go without them. But the drafters of the DSA’s programmatic amendment tell us it isn’t literal. “Abolishing the police and prison system” is merely a shorthand. It translates roughly to “abolishing prisons and police as they exist under capitalism.” Hazel Williams, a driving force behind the amendment, assures this doesn’t foreclose “some community force under communism” that promotes accountability. She cites approvingly the Paris Commune that, according to Karl Marx, turned the cops into its responsible agents. In other words, according to Williams, there can still be “police” as we ordinarily use that word. She even leaves open the possibility of separating people “hellbent on committing violence” from those “they intend to hurt.” Separation, you say? That sounds an awful lot like prison. Williams isn’t against, in ordinary English, “prisons” and “police.” She’s against prisons and police under capitalism , “as institutions of capitalist domination.” The issue, then, is not badged officers or constables. It’s capitalist domination that Williams truly opposes. And that position is almost ubiquitous within the organization. The DSA, as the name suggests, is an avowedly socialist outfit. It opposes capitalism, which its program already makes abundantly clear. The very first line asks workers to “[i]magine… a future without capitalism.” Later, it states that its enemy is “the entire global system of capital.” Elsewhere, the program calls “for ending capitalist oligarchy.” If the amendment on “abolishing… police and prison” simply amounts to a disavowal of capitalism, it adds nothing. But it’s worse than that, because the amendment isn’t mere surplusage. It sows confusion. Anyone reading “abolishing… police and prison” will understandably assume that cops and incarceration are a no-go. But, according to Williams, that plain meaning isn’t what the amendment is saying. Drafters made this disconnect all but inevitable. The amendment originally mentioned “abolishing the carceral forces of the capitalist state.” Drafters “simplified” it to “abolishing the police and prison system.” Their simplification erased the words that carried the meaning. Williams bristles at those who view abolition as “an abstract proposition that all coercion must vanish forever” — and fair enough. That’s an unjustified interpretation. But expect a broader audience to interpret “abolish prisons/police” literally. That is the natural reading. If that’s not your message, you aren’t expressing yourself well. Don’t use a totalizing word like “abolition” unless you mean it. Many leftists don’t mean it, but insist on using the word anyway. They’re married to it — and stuck in the haze of 2020. COVID-era progressivism didn’t birth abolition. The idea existed for decades, with the DSA officially endorsing it in 2017. But 2020 brought a peculiar obsession with slogans at the expense of clear, effective messaging. This milieu moved abolishing prisons and police from the academic fringes to the mainstream. Calling for abolition became so fashionable that, years later, people still insist on using the word despite its political toxicity. Living in the most dangerous developed nation on Earth, vast majorities of Americans think that crime is a serious problem. Dismantling the criminal justice system will strike them as a surefire way to invite more danger into their lives. The DSA saying it wants to abolish prisons and police will thus dampen its appeal and fuel allegations of extremism. It’ll especially sabotage outreach to the working class, whose communities are most ravaged by crime. These people should be the DSA’s primary constituency, and are those whose interests its economic platform serves most. If it cannot get them on board, that spells doom for the movement. Abolition is bad policy. It may be worse politics, as evidenced by its underwater poll numbers, even among those who identify as very left-leaning. Of course, public concern cuts both ways. Police malfeasance and squalid, overcrowded prisons are also legitimate and widespread worries. These are serious societal failures that, like crime, hit the working class hardest. But addressing those failures neither requires nor warrants eliminating prisons and police entirely. Reform is an option, and it’s what most Americans want. Polls show that the vast majority believe the police system is at least somewhat sound but needs improvements. Americans similarly admire how prisons isolate dangerous individuals and reject abolition while desiring better, more rehabilitative conditions. Plenty support shifting certain carceral funds toward welfare spending. These are demands the DSA could champion with broad support — and, to some extent, already does. Its program, after all, calls for “redirecting funding to public services.” But what follows — “as [a step] toward abolishing the police and prison system” — overshadows it. The finalized amendment makes it sound like the DSA’s vision requires abandoning the most important tools of criminal justice. Democratic socialism in the public imagination, then, becomes even more anathema to safety and order. That not only reinforces a blatant falsehood but is a gift to the Right. Such generosity is unwarranted. “Abolition” is not a magic word. The DSA doesn’t have to use it. And it shouldn’t. Eliminating prisons and police, which are socially necessary, is an unworthy goal. But, if you’re going to call for that anyway, at least mean it. The drafters don’t, yet still issue the call. It’s the worst of both worlds. For a medicine they aren’t prescribing, the movement suffers side effects all the same.
